CONTACT US:
Complaints? Video submissions? Sponsorships? Collabs? Business inquires? 
Email our board at mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com. 

BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect.

The suspect who opened fire was Matthew McCulloch, an off-duty St. Louis County Police Officer from Missouri. He fired 12 shots into the air at North Kirkwood Middle School, school during what his attorneys described as a bipolar manic episode. Matthew is also the son of longtime St. Louis County Prosecutor Bob McCulloch, who left the position in 2018, and he is the nephew of current St. Charles County Prosecutor, Joe McCulloch. Immediately following the incident, Matthew was taken into custody and was quickly fired from the police department, where he had been working since 2017. He was initially charged with five counts of armed criminal action, four counts of endangering the welfare of a child, one count of terroristic threat and one count of unlawful use of a weapon, totaling 11 felony counts. In January 2025, Matthew took a plea deal, pleading guilty to six counts of endangering the welfare of a child, one count of making a terroristic threat, and one count of unlawful use of a weapon, totaling eight felony counts. On March 27, 2025, Judge Ellen Ribaduo sentenced Matthew to five years of supervised probation. His probation terms include no contact with victims, random drug testing, mandatory therapy, sobriety, a ban on firearm possession, and regular court check-ins. No prison time included in the sentence has sparked backlash from parents who were present at the scene. Many of them believe Matthew's familial ties to prosecutors could have influenced his sentence. One parent says his job was to protect people, and he came from a family that knows the system. The judge who sentenced him has expressed safety concerns if Matthew were to be jailed due to his ties to law enforcement and prosecutors. She also believes Matthew could be more closely monitored under probation, noting that public safety would be maintained through strict oversight. Let us know what you think about the judge's decision in the comments below. There's nothing more terrifying than realizing the person sworn to protect can unravel in the middle of an event. The fire 12 rounds into the sky and still walk away with a sentence that makes parents wonder if justice has two different settings, depending on your last name. Some people think cops are carved out of cinder blocks like nothing shakes us, but reality is much ugly. And this job cuts into you every year into the pain doesn't even show in your face anymore. And cops actually crack in silence long before anyone sees the signs and a uniform can take. high damage until it spills out in front of families who had no way to see it coming. I think mandatory psychological exams should be a yearly appointment because truth be told, they're just as serious as firearm qualifications. You cannot throw officers into trauma for years, ignore the warning signs, and then shrug it off when a manic break nearly turns a children's event into a tragedy. I've seated in Philly, cops fall apart quietly because they know the system treats mental health like a liability, so they hide it. Right up until the moment it explodes. That's why communities need officers who are grounded, not officers drowning in untreated mental health issues. And a badge doesn't erase bipolar episodes, trauma, or personal demons. It just masked them behind authority. And that mask did slip here and it shook these people because the danger did come from someone parents would have trusted without hesitation. Because when a cop's mind caves in and no one catches it, the threat isn't a stranger in the dark. Unfortunately, it's the officer family's trust to stand between them and the danger.
